column1: Six weaknesses, three changes, one night. Fix the ones the attacker was actually going to use

How to play: every weakness on the list is real and every one is worth fixing eventually. You only get three changes before the attack. Pick the three that block it. Anything you leave undone gets used, or turns out not to have mattered tonight.
/* Harden First - AP Networking Topic 1.4, sub-skills 2.C and 2.D.
Topic 1.4 lists a dozen things a user ""should"" do, and a list like that
teaches nothing about priority. Real hardening is triage: limited time,
everything is worth doing, and only some of it blocks tonight's attack.
So the scarcity is the mechanic. Three of the six weaknesses on each site
are on the attack path and three are genuinely lower priority THAT NIGHT,
which is a different claim from ""not worth fixing"" and the debrief says so.
EK 1.4.B.5 (default credentials) is the one that recurs, because it is the
single highest-value fix and students consistently rank it below password

{ t: 'Change the router admin password from the default', d: 'It is still the password printed in the manual', key: true },
{ t: 'Switch wireless encryption from WPA2 to WPA3', d: 'The hardware supports it', key: true },
{ t: 'Set a long unique wireless passphrase', d: 'Currently eight lowercase letters', key: true },
{ t: 'Rename the SSID so it does not say the router model', d: 'It broadcasts the make and model', key: false },
{ t: 'Turn on the monthly firmware update check', d: 'Firmware is current as of today', key: false },

{ needs: 2, txt: 'Guessed the eight-character passphrase from a wordlist in under a minute' }

why: 'The three that mattered were the three on the way in: the admin password, the encryption, and the passphrase. Renaming the SSID and updating firmware are both good practice and neither would have stopped anything tonight, because the attacker never needed to know the model and the firmware was already current.'
scene: 'A staff member clicked a convincing invoice email this morning and typed their password into the page it opened.',
{ t: 'Turn on multi-factor authentication for staff accounts', d: 'Currently password only', key: true },
{ t: 'Force a password reset for the account that was phished', d: 'The password is now known to someone else', key: true },
{ t: 'Check whether that password was reused on other systems', d: 'Reuse is common', key: true },
{ t: 'Increase the minimum password length to 14', d: 'Currently 10', key: false },

{ needs: 1, txt: 'Kept using the stolen password because it was never changed' },
{ needs: 2, txt: 'Used the same password to open the finance system as well' }

why: 'When a password is already stolen, length and lockout do nothing at all: the attacker is not guessing, they are typing the correct password. Multi-factor blocks them, a reset invalidates what they hold, and checking reuse finds the other doors that same password opens.'

{ t: 'Put a passphrase and WPA3 on the wireless network', d: 'Currently open, no encryption', key: true },
{ t: 'Move printers and cameras off the staff network', d: 'Everything is on one flat network', key: true },

{ needs: 0, txt: 'Joined the open network from the flat upstairs and read unencrypted traffic' },
{ needs: 1, txt: 'Reached the file share directly, because nothing separated devices from each other' },
{ needs: 2, txt: 'Logged in to the camera with admin and admin and watched the office' }

why: 'Hiding an SSID is the fix people reach for first and it is close to worthless, because a scanner sees the network anyway. Encryption keeps outsiders off, segmentation stops whoever does get on from reaching everything, and default camera credentials are the reason a camera is usually the first device an intruder owns.'

{ t: 'Require a VPN for anything work related off site', d: 'Untrusted networks between here and there', key: true },
{ t: 'Turn on the host firewall', d: 'Currently off because it blocked a printer once', key: true },

{ t: 'Add the laptop to the asset register', d: 'Paperwork, worth doing', key: false },
{ t: 'Set a screensaver timeout of 15 minutes', d: 'Better than nothing, slow to matter', key: false }

why: 'On an untrusted network the device has to defend itself, because you no longer control anything between it and the internet. Encrypt the traffic, close the ports, and patch the known hole. A screensaver timeout helps against the person walking past, which is a real threat but not this one.'
scene: 'A contractor needs access to one shared folder for two weeks. IT is about to hand them a normal staff account.',

Eight builds, eight address blocks. Give each one room to grow and not one address more

How to play: each build tells you how many hosts a segment must hold. Pick the smallest subnet that fits them. A block that is too small strands devices with no address. A block that is too big is not wrong on the day, but it burns addresses you cannot get back and it is the answer the exam marks down.
/* Subnet Sprint - AP Networking Topic 3.4, sub-skill 2.C.
EK 3.4.C.3 gives the host count as 2^n - 2, and EK 3.4.C.4 says the right
subnet is ""the smallest possible network size that accommodates the required
number of hosts"". That second sentence is the whole game. A /24 fits nearly
every case offered here, so a student who only checks ""does it fit"" scores
badly and finds out why. The two reserved addresses are the network address
and the broadcast address, which is where the minus two comes from and why
a segment of exactly 30 hosts does NOT fit in a /27. */
why: 'A /28 leaves 16 addresses and 14 usable, which covers 12 with two spare. A /27 would also fit, but it hands out 30 usable addresses to a room that needs 12.' },

why: 'This is the trap. A /27 gives 32 addresses but only 30 USABLE, and the first and last are the network and broadcast addresses. Thirty devices need thirty usable, so exactly 30 fits only if you have 30 usable, and you do. A /27 is correct here and a /26 wastes half the block.' },
{ who: 'Student laptops, one wing', need: 100, base: '172.16.8.0',
why: 'A /25 gives 128 addresses and 126 usable. A /26 gives only 62 and strands 38 laptops with no address at all.' },
why: 'A /30 gives exactly 2 usable addresses. It is the smallest useful subnet and it is what point-to-point links use for the same reason.' },
{ who: 'Guest wireless at an event', need: 400, base: '10.20.0.0',
why: 'A /23 gives 512 addresses and 510 usable. A /24 caps out at 254 and would turn away more than a third of the guests.' },
why: 'A /29 gives 8 addresses and 6 usable, which is exactly six printers. Tight, correct, and the reason to leave growth room in the PLAN rather than in every subnet.' },
{ who: 'Lab benches, every seat wired', need: 63, base: '172.20.4.0',

why: 'One short. A /26 gives 64 addresses but only 62 usable, and 63 benches need 63. Losing the network and broadcast addresses is exactly what pushes this over the line into a /25, and it is the commonest off-by-one in subnetting.' },
why: 'Two routers, two addresses, a /30. Handing a link a /24 is the single commonest waste in a real address plan.' }

The rules are all correct. Only the order is wrong, and the order is what decides who gets in

How to play: a firewall reads its list from the top and stops at the FIRST rule that matches. Every rule below a broader one that already matched is dead. Move the rules with the arrows until the traffic below behaves the way the goal asks, then run it.
/* Rule Order - AP Networking Topic 3.5, sub-skill 2.C.
EK 3.5.C.4: ""Firewall rules are implemented in order, and changing the order
of a set of rules can change which traffic is permitted."" That sentence
cannot be assessed by a question with no ordering in it, which is why this
game exists and why the quiz version of this topic cannot replace it.
Every case ships with rules that are individually correct. The only defect
is sequence, so a student cannot score by spotting a ""wrong"" rule. */
goal: 'Let the office subnet reach the file server on port 445, and block every other machine from it.',
{ id: 'a', txt: 'deny any -> 10.0.5.10 port 445', act: 'deny', hits: ['t1', 't2'] },
{ id: 't1', pk: 'Office PC 10.0.1.44 -> file server :445', want: 'permit' },
{ id: 't2', pk: 'Guest laptop 10.0.9.7 -> file server :445', want: 'deny' }

why: 'A deny that names ""any"" matches the office PC too. Placed first, it shadows the permit completely and the file server becomes unreachable for everyone, which reads as a broken server rather than a firewall problem. The specific permit has to sit above the broad deny.'
goal: 'Block the one compromised host, but leave the rest of its subnet working normally.',

why: 'The subnet-wide permit matches the infected host as well, because .99 is inside 172.16.4.0/24. Quarantine rules are always more specific than the rule they carve an exception out of, so they always go above it.'
goal: 'Allow web traffic out, allow the mail server out, and deny everything else leaving the network.',
{ id: 'a', txt: 'deny any -> any', act: 'deny', hits: ['t1', 't2', 't3'] },
{ id: 'b', txt: 'permit any -> any port 443', act: 'permit', hits: ['t1'] },
{ id: 'c', txt: 'permit 10.0.2.25 -> any port 25', act: 'permit', hits: ['t2'] }

why: 'The catch-all deny is not wrong, it is just last. Its whole job is to be the rule nothing else matched, which is why it is called the implicit deny and why writing it at the top switches the network off. The two permits do not overlap, so either of them may come first.'
goal: 'Let the IT admin subnet manage the switch over SSH. Nobody else may reach the switch at all.',
{ id: 'a', txt: 'deny any -> 10.0.0.2 any port', act: 'deny', hits: ['t1', 't2', 't3'] },

why: 'Note the third packet. Because the permit names only port 22, the broad deny below it still catches every other port on the same device, which is exactly what you want. Specific permit first, broad deny second, and the deny keeps doing useful work.'
goal: 'Guests reach the internet. Guests never reach anything internal. Internal machines talk to each other freely.',

why: 'This is the guest network in three lines. ""Permit guests to any"" includes the internal network, because internal addresses are part of any. The narrower deny has to come first, and then the broad permit does what people assume it does.'

broad rule was assumed to match any packet whose intended rule sat below it.
Exhaustive permutation testing caught it. If a case has more than one correct
ordering, this model says so honestly instead of insisting on one answer. */
